fetched_contents.text: Dizziness: Causes & Treatment How is dizziness treated? Dizziness treatment depends on the cause. For example, if you’re dizzy because you have an inner ear infection, your healthcare provider will treat the infection. If you’re taking medications that make you feel dizzy, your provider may recommend you limit activities until your body adjusts to the medication. Some people benefit from a vestibular test battery to help determine if dizziness is due to an inner ear problem and vestibular rehabilitation therapy (VRT) to help treat the dizziness. Vestibular rehabilitation therapy involves exercises to manage dizziness symptoms. Can I treat dizziness at home? No, but you can manage dizziness. If you’re feeling dizzy, lie down until dizziness passes. When you get up, be sure to move slowly and carefully. What are the possible complications or risks of not treating dizziness? Dizziness may not seem as if it’s a symptom of a serious issue, but you should still talk to a healthcare provider if you’re frequently dizzy: * Dizziness may be a symptom of medical conditions that could get worse if left untreated. * Dizziness is a balance issue, increasing your risk of falling and possibly being injured. * Dizziness may make it unsafe for you to drive vehicles. * Sometimes, dizziness may make it hard for you to work or manage your daily tasks and responsibilities. Can dizziness be prevented? The best way to prevent dizziness is to find out why you’re dizzy. For example, if you become dizzy when you’re dehydrated, you may prevent dizziness by drinking enough water. If you take blood pressure medication that makes you dizzy, your healthcare provider may prescribe a different medication or dosage. Unfortunately, you can’t predict or prevent all things that cause dizziness, such as a neurological disorder.

This content does not have an Arabic version. * Diseases & Conditions Low blood pressure (hypotension) Request an Appointment Print Overview Low blood pressure is a condition in which the force of the blood pushing against the artery walls is too low. It's also called hypotension. Blood pressure is measured in millimeters of mercury (mm Hg). In general, low blood pressure is a reading lower than 90/60 mm Hg. What's considered low blood pressure for one person might be OK for someone else though. Low blood pressure might cause no symptoms that you notice. Or it might cause dizziness and fainting. Sometimes, low blood pressure can be life-threatening. The causes of low blood pressure include dehydration and other serious medical conditions. It's important to find out what's causing low blood pressure so that it can be treated, if needed. Types Types of low blood pressure include: * Orthostatic hypotension, also called postural hypotension. This is a sudden drop in blood pressure when standing up after sitting or lying down. Causes include dehydration, long-term bed rest, pregnancy, certain medical conditions and some medicines. This type of low blood pressure is common in older adults. * Postprandial hypotension. This drop in blood pressure occurs 1 to 2 hours after eating. It's most likely to affect older adults, especially those with high blood pressure. The risk also is higher for older adults with Parkinson's disease or other conditions that affect the part of the nervous system that controls automatic functions such as breathing and heart rate. This is called the autonomic nervous system. Certain lifestyle changes might help ease symptoms of postprandial hypotension. Eat small, low-carbohydrate meals, drink more water, and stay away from alcohol. * Neurally mediated hypotension. This is a blood pressure drop that happens after standing for long amounts of time. This type of low blood pressure mostly affects young adults and children. It might result from communication trouble between the heart and the brain. * Multiple system atrophy with orthostatic hypotension. This rare condition affects the autonomic nervous system. Multiple system atrophy with orthostatic hypotension is linked with having very high blood pressure while lying down. It also used to be called Shy-Drager syndrome. These can happen for reasons such as serious bleeding, serious infections or allergic reactions. Extreme low blood pressure can lead to a condition known as shock. Symptoms of shock include: * Confusion, especially in older people. * Cold, clammy skin. * Decrease in skin color, also called pallor. * Rapid, shallow breathing. * Weak and rapid pulse. When to see a doctor If you have symptoms of extreme low blood pressure or shock, call 911 or your local emergency number. fetched_contents.text: If You Are Experiencing Dizziness First, remain calm. If you have a family member or friend nearby, make sure they are with you now. If this is a new problem for you, the key question is whether you should call 911 and go immediately to the emergency room. If you are dizzy right now and have any of the following neurological symptoms along with your dizziness or vertigo, call 911 immediately: * New confusion or trouble speaking or understanding speech * New slurred speech or hoarseness of voice * New numbness or weakness of the face, arm, or leg * New clumsiness or tremor (shaking) of the arms or legs * New trouble seeing out of one or both eyes, or to one side * New double vision or inability to move one or both eyes * New unequal pupils or drooping eyelid on one side * New inability to stand even when holding onto something firm * Sudden severe vomiting with no known cause * Sudden severe headache or neck pain with no known cause Dizziness, Stroke and TIA Even if you don't have any of the symptoms above, you could still be having a stroke or have suffered a recent pre-stroke (transient ischemic attack or TIA). A stroke or TIA is more likely if you are older or have known stroke risk factors (such as smoking, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, sickle cell disease, or a personal or family history of stroke or heart attacks). But even young people with none of these traditional stroke risk factors can still suffer a stroke. Furthermore, there are dangerous heart conditions (heart attack or cardiac arrhythmia) that can also cause dizziness or vertigo. If you do not already know the cause of your new dizziness or vertigo, call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room to be assessed. The only definite way to know you have not suffered a stroke or TIA is to be sure that you know that your dizziness or vertigo is due to something less serious. The most common conditions are benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), vestibular migraine, Menière’s disease and vestibular neuritis/labyrinthitis. Unfortunately, each of these conditions can produce symptoms very similar to those of stroke or TIA, so careful attention to symptom details is required. Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV) If the dizziness or vertigo symptoms follow any of the following patterns, the cause is likely BPPV: (1) symptoms are intermittent; (2) symptoms occur only when the head is tipped or moved in a particular direction (especially when rolling over in bed to one side); (3) symptoms last for less than a minute after the head position change as long as the head is held still and (4) there is no vomiting, hearing loss or neurological symptoms. Although rare exceptions do occur, people with these symptom patterns usually do not have strokes. People experiencing these symptoms should contact their primary physician for advice. Vestibular Migraine and Menière’s Disease If the dizziness or vertigo comes in episodes that last for minutes to hours, it could be due to vestibular migraine (usually without hearing symptoms) or Menière’s disease (usually with hearing symptoms), but it also can be the result of a pre-stroke (transient ischemic attack, or TIA). Those who have had such symptoms repeatedly over many years usually do not have TIA, but when the first episode occurs, it is advisable to seek medical care right away to assess your immediate risk for stroke. If there are obvious neurological symptoms (described in detail above), call 911 or proceed immediately to the emergency room. If there are no obvious neurological symptoms, it is reasonable for patients to contact their primary physician for advice. Vestibular Neuritis and Labyrinthitis If the dizziness or vertigo is new, severe and persists for hours to days; has not stopped; and is associated with vomiting and trouble walking, it could be due to vestibular neuritis (usually without hearing symptoms) or labyrinthitis (usually with hearing symptoms). This symptom complex is identical to the symptoms seen with strokes in the balance part of the brain (brainstem or cerebellum), and it is impossible to exclude stroke without careful examination of the patient’s eye movements. Even without neurological symptoms, patients with this symptom complex should generally call 911 or proceed directly to the emergency room to get immediate help. There, patients with this acute vestibular syndrome should expect the examiner to carefully inspect their eyes, including performing a test with a rapid head turn to either side while the patient looks straight ahead (head impulse test). This test can be performed with or without a special diagnostic device (quantitative video-oculography) sometimes referred to as “stroke goggles.” When performed properly and combined with two other eye exams (together called “HINTS”), this exam can confirm vestibular neuritis rather than stroke. This approach has been shown to be more accurate than brain imaging in several scientific studies. Although it is common for patients to undergo CT scan of the brain in this setting, CT is generally unhelpful and risks radiation exposure. If neuroimaging is required, this should generally be by MRI scan of the brain.

Likely causes and when they are worrisome

Common non-urgent causes such as dehydration or low blood pressure are among the most frequent explanations for dizziness and lightheadedness. Mayoclinic notes that low blood pressure can be caused by dehydration, long-term bed rest, pregnancy, certain medical conditions, and some medicines, and it can cause dizziness and fainting [N2-F2]. Harvard Health similarly lists dehydration, medication side effects, sudden blood pressure drops, low blood sugar, and heart disease or stroke as possible causes of lightheadedness [N2-R2]. Women’s Health Services explains that lightheadedness often occurs when you get up too quickly from a seated or lying position and notes that a quick drop in blood pressure and blood flow to the head can be the trigger [N2-R3]. MedlinePlus adds that a sudden drop in blood pressure or dehydration can make you dizzy, reinforcing that these are everyday, non-urgent causes [N2-R5]. So, if the dizziness is brief, tied to position change, or linked to something like standing up fast or mild dehydration, it is more likely to be a routine issue than a serious one [N2-R3][N2-R5].

Red flags that point to stroke, heart attack, or inner ear problems are much more concerning. The stroke warning signs are especially important: sudden trouble walking, dizziness, loss of balance, lack of coordination, sudden trouble seeing, sudden numbness or weakness in the face, arm, or leg, and slurred speech or difficulty in speech [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The American Stroke Association emphasizes the B.E. F.A.S.T. warning signs and notes that stroke survivor stories often involve sudden symptoms like face drooping and difficulty walking or dizziness [N3-F3]. NHS also says that TIA symptoms are the same as stroke symptoms, but they last only a few minutes or hours and are a warning sign that a stroke may be possible or likely [N3-R5]. In addition, Johns Hopkins Medicine warns that dizziness plus confusion, trouble speaking or understanding speech, numbness or weakness of the face, arm, or leg, trouble walking, severe headache, vomiting, or unequal pupils may indicate stroke or TIA and should prompt immediate 911 care [N4-F4]. The article also highlights that dangerous heart conditions such as heart attack or cardiac arrhythmia can cause dizziness or vertigo [N4-F4]. This means dizziness is worrisome when it comes with neurological symptoms, new weakness, speech issues, balance problems, or when it occurs alongside severe headache, vomiting, or sudden severe neck pain [N3-R1][N3-R2][N4-F4].

How to distinguish ordinary dizziness from something more serious depends on the context and associated symptoms. Ordinary dizziness is often brief, related to position change, dehydration, or temporary blood pressure drops, and can be managed by lying down and moving slowly [N2-R3][N2-R5]. However, it becomes serious when it is new, severe, persistent, or accompanied by neurological symptoms, vomiting, trouble walking, confusion, or speech changes [N4-F4]. The Johns Hopkins article explains that some conditions, such as vestibular neuritis or labyrinthitis, can produce symptoms very similar to stroke or TIA, so careful attention to symptom details is needed [N4-F4]. That means it is not enough to rely on dizziness alone; the key is whether the episode is isolated or whether it is part of a pattern that suggests a neurological, cardiac, or inner ear emergency [N4-F4]. In short, if the dizziness is brief and only happens after standing up quickly, it is more likely ordinary, but if it is sudden, severe, or associated with any of the red flags above, it is much more likely serious [N2-R3][N3-R1][N4-F4].

## Likely causes: ordinary vs. worrisome

The evidence shows that dizziness and lightheadedness can have many causes, and the seriousness depends on what is happening.

### Common non-urgent causes
The most common non-urgent causes are things like **dehydration, low blood pressure, sudden blood pressure drops, low blood sugar, and heart disease or stroke** [N2-R2]. Mayoclinic also notes that low blood pressure can be caused by dehydration, long-term bed rest, pregnancy, certain medical conditions, and some medicines, and that it can cause dizziness and fainting [N2-F2]. So if the dizziness is brief, tied to position change, or linked to something like standing up fast or mild dehydration, it is more likely a routine issue than a serious one [N2-R3][N2-R5].

Once the episode passes, resume normal activity slowly and stay alert. Cleveland Clinic says to move slowly and carefully when getting up and to avoid activities that could be unsafe if you are dizzy [N1-F1]. MyHealth Alberta advises sitting up slowly and then standing slowly after lying down [N1-R3]. If dizziness recurs, is persistent, or is not easily explained, you should ask for tests or ongoing evaluation. NHS says that TIA symptoms are the same as stroke symptoms, but they last only a few minutes or hours and are a warning sign that a stroke may be possible or likely [N3-R5]. Johns Hopkins Medicine adds that dizziness plus confusion, trouble speaking or understanding speech, numbness or weakness of the face, arm, or leg, trouble walking, severe headache, vomiting, or unequal pupils may indicate stroke or TIA and should prompt immediate 911 care [N4-F4]. It also warns that dangerous heart conditions such as **heart attack or cardiac arrhythmia** can cause dizziness or vertigo [N4-F4].

So the key distinction is this: ordinary dizziness is often **brief, position-related, or linked to dehydration**, while worrisome dizziness is **new, severe, persistent, or associated with neurological symptoms such as confusion, speech changes, weakness, or balance problems** [N2-R3][N3-R1][N4-F4]. If you’re unsure whether the episode is ordinary or serious, the safest answer is to treat it as a possible emergency and seek care promptly [N4-F4].

## What to do after the episode: next steps

### When to contact a doctor versus when to go to the emergency room
If the episode is new, severe, persistent, or associated with neurological symptoms, you should **call 911 or go to the emergency room** [N4-F4]. Mayo Clinic says that if dizziness is occasional and does not cause significant problems, you may not need treatment, but it is still important to see a healthcare professional to find out the cause [N2-F2]. HealthDirect advises seeking urgent care if you feel lightheaded or faint while sitting or lying down, or if you faint more than once [N5-R2]. Cleveland Clinic and My Health Alberta both emphasize that you should contact a doctor if you are frequently dizzy or if symptoms interfere with daily life [N1-F1][N1-R3]. Johns Hopkins Medicine says if the dizziness is new and not obvious, you should call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room to be assessed [N4-F4]. So the rule of thumb is: **routine doctor visits are for recurring or mild dizziness; emergency care is for new, severe, or neurological episodes** [N2-F2][N5-R2][N4-F4].

### What information to record about the episode
To help your doctor understand what is going on, keep track of several details. Mayo Clinic recommends recording your symptoms, when they occur, and what you were doing at the time [N2-F2]. Cleveland Clinic says to tell the doctor when you feel dizzy, whether you also feel faint or lightheaded, and what activities or situations seem to trigger it [N5-R1]. My Health Alberta similarly says to note when you feel dizzy and any associated symptoms [N5-R4]. Johns Hopkins Medicine emphasizes documenting neurological symptoms such as confusion, trouble speaking, numbness, weakness, and trouble walking [N4-F4]. The best information to record is: **when it happened, how long it lasted, what you were doing, any associated symptoms, and whether it came back** [N2-F2][N5-R1][N5-R4][N4-F4].

### Practical steps to take after symptoms improve
Once the episode passes, resume normal activity slowly and stay alert. Cleveland Clinic says to move slowly and carefully when getting up and to avoid activities that could be unsafe if you are dizzy [N1-F1]. MyHealth Alberta advises sitting up slowly and then standing slowly after lying down [N1-R3]. ENT Care adds that once dizziness has subsided, avoid sudden movements and bright lights and loud sounds [N6-R5]. Johns Hopkins Medicine also says to remain calm, stay with a companion if possible, and note any neurological symptoms that develop [N4-F4]. The overall message is to **resume activity gradually and keep the episode in mind, because dizziness can recur and a second episode may change the diagnosis** [N1-F1][N1-R3][N6-R5][N4-F4].

## What to do if symptoms recur or persist over time

If dizziness comes back after resting, treat it the same way as the first episode: **sit or lie down safely, stay still, and move slowly** [N1-F1][N1-R3]. If the symptoms last for hours or days, the urgency increases. Johns Hopkins Medicine says that if the dizziness or vertigo is new, severe, and persists for hours to days, especially if associated with vomiting and trouble walking, it could be serious and should be evaluated right away [N4-F4]. It also says that if the dizziness is not fleeting and balance is compromised, you should immediately visit the closest emergency department [N4-R2]. The Cleveland Clinic notes that dizziness can be caused by inner ear disorders and that some people benefit from vestibular testing and therapy [N1-R3]. MyHealth Alberta says to sit or lie down right away when you feel dizzy and to fall-proof your home [N6-R2]. The key takeaway is that **persistent or recurring dizziness should prompt medical evaluation because it may point to an inner ear disorder, a neurological problem, or a condition that needs ongoing treatment** [N1-R3][N4-F4][N6-R2].

### When to ask about tests or ongoing evaluation
If dizziness recurs, is persistent, or is not easily explained, you should ask for tests or ongoing evaluation. Mayo Clinic says that if dizziness is frequent, it is important to talk to a healthcare provider to find out the cause [N2-F2]. Cleveland Clinic also says that dizziness may be a symptom of medical conditions that could get worse if left untreated [N1-F1]. HealthDirect says to seek urgent care if you feel lightheaded or faint while sitting or lying down or if you faint more than once [N5-R2]. Johns Hopkins Medicine says that if dizziness is new and not obvious, you should call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room [N4-F4]. So the evidence supports asking for tests or ongoing evaluation when symptoms **recur, are persistent, or are associated with neurological symptoms, balance issues, or other concerning features** [N2-F2][N1-F1][N5-R2][N4-F4].

## Bottom line

If you’re feeling really dizzy and kinda lightheaded, the safest first step is to **sit or lie down immediately and stay still** [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-R4][N1-R5]. If the episode is severe, worsening, or associated with neurological symptoms, **call 911 or go to the emergency room** [N4-F4]. If it is brief and linked to position change or dehydration, it may be ordinary, but you should still consider it serious enough to talk to a doctor [N2-R3][N2-R5][N4-F4]. After the episode, record the time, duration, associated symptoms, and any triggers, and resume normal activity slowly [N2-F2][N5-R1][N5-R4][N4-F4]. If the dizziness comes back or persists, do not ignore it; ask for tests or ongoing evaluation because recurring dizziness may signal something more serious [N2-F2][N4-F4][N6-R2].

In short: **safe, slow, and careful management is the priority now. If in doubt, go to the emergency room. If symptoms are ordinary, still see a doctor to find out why** [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F4].
